2026-11-06 | Lab 11" author: "Jess Helmer" footer: "[jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/)" format: revealjs: code-link: true slide-number: true code-line-numbers: false theme: ../../gt-theme.scss width: 1200 css: contrast-slide-styling.css execute: echo: true dpi: 600 freeze: auto knitr: opts_chunk: dev: svg --- ## Outline - Repeated measures ANOVA - Multilevel modeling ::: {.cell} ::: # Repeated Measures ANOVA ## Repeated Measures ANOVA It is sometimes the case that we have *repeated measures* data ::: subpoint ○ Responses collected on the same measure for the same subjects more than one time ::: Some examples of repeated measures data are... ::: subpoint ○ A mental health screening questionnaire given to participants once per day ::: ::: subpoint ○ A yearly customer satisfaction survey ::: For these designs, we have to consider if conditions are **between-person** or **within-person**. ## Repeated Measures Model ## Repeated Measures Example :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="85%"} Remember the chick dataset from Lab 06? We are going to use... another chick dataset! Instead of having one value of chick weight for each chick, this one tracks chicks over time. We will have weekly updates on each chick's weight. ::: ::: {.column width="15%"} ![](https://mannapro.com/cdn/shop/articles/how-to-raise-baby-chickens_2x_b6a71ebc-2d08-4bdc-82b0-18ccf861c9bd.jpg?v=1740003489) ::: :::: ## Repeated Measures Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data <- read_csv(here::here("lab", "data", "lab_11", "chick_week_data.csv")) chick_data ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 180 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 13 1 0 60 2 13 1 1 71 3 13 1 2 91 4 13 1 3 96 5 9 1 0 68 6 9 1 1 90 7 9 1 2 100 8 9 1 3 98 9 20 1 0 58 10 20 1 1 77 # ℹ 170 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Repeated Measures Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("psych") psych::describe(chick_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` vars n mean sd median trimmed mad min max range skew kurtosis chick 1 180 26.09 14.56 27.0 26.24 19.27 1 50 49 -0.11 -1.18 diet 2 180 2.27 1.15 2.0 2.21 1.48 1 4 3 0.27 -1.39 week 3 180 1.50 1.12 1.5 1.50 1.48 0 3 3 0.00 -1.38 weight 4 180 159.48 78.37 147.5 151.85 92.66 58 373 315 0.64 -0.55 se chick 1.09 diet 0.09 week 0.08 weight 5.84 ``` ::: ::: ## Repeated Measures Example We want to estimate the effect of week of the experiment on chick weight! Is `week` a between- or within-subject (chick) factor? [Within!]{.fragment} [First, notice that all the variables in this dataset are `double`s (decimal point numbers). The ANOVA functions want to treat these as `factor`s.]{.fragment} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned <- chick_data |> mutate(chick = factor(chick), week = factor(week), diet = factor(diet)) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned <- chick_data |> mutate( across(c(chick, week, diet), factor) ) ``` ::: ::: :::: ## Aside: `across()` `across()` is a helpful function that can be used within functions like `summarize()` and `mutate()`. When we want to apply the same transformation to multiple columns, we can target them all with `across()` and specify the transformation once, instead of manually specifying each one. `across(columns, function(s))` ::: subpoint ○ `columns` = `` columns to target ::: ::: subpoint ○ `function(s)` = name of function to use, *anonymous function*, or list of functions. ::: ## Aside: `across()` Examples of `across()`... ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Name of Function Just like we did before ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data |> mutate(across(c(chick, week, diet), factor)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 180 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 13 1 0 60 2 13 1 1 71 3 13 1 2 91 4 13 1 3 96 5 9 1 0 68 6 9 1 1 90 7 9 1 2 100 8 9 1 3 98 9 20 1 0 58 10 20 1 1 77 # ℹ 170 more rows ``` ::: ::: ### Anonymous Function Example of standardizing across all columns (not necessarily helpful here). Reminder: within `function()`, `column` just serves as a placeholder name for that column. You can name this whatever you want, as long as you use the same name within the actual function part. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data |> mutate(across(everything(), function(column) (column - mean(column)) / sd(column))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 180 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 -0.899 -1.11 -1.34 -1.27 2 -0.899 -1.11 -0.446 -1.13 3 -0.899 -1.11 0.446 -0.874 4 -0.899 -1.11 1.34 -0.810 5 -1.17 -1.11 -1.34 -1.17 6 -1.17 -1.11 -0.446 -0.887 7 -1.17 -1.11 0.446 -0.759 8 -1.17 -1.11 1.34 -0.784 9 -0.418 -1.11 -1.34 -1.29 10 -0.418 -1.11 -0.446 -1.05 # ℹ 170 more rows ``` ::: ::: ### List of Functions Example of summarizing columns by multiple functions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data |> summarize( across( where(is.numeric), list(min = min, max = max, mean = function(column) mean(column, na.rm = T)) ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 12 chick_min chick_max chick_mean diet_min diet_max diet_mean week_min week_max 1 1 50 26.1 1 4 2.27 0 3 # ℹ 4 more variables: week_mean , weight_min , weight_max , # weight_mean ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Aside: `across()` Our original `across()` method successfully converted the intended columns to `factor()`s. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned <- chick_data |> mutate( across(c(chick, week, diet), factor) ) chick_cleaned ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 180 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 13 1 0 60 2 13 1 1 71 3 13 1 2 91 4 13 1 3 96 5 9 1 0 68 6 9 1 1 90 7 9 1 2 100 8 9 1 3 98 9 20 1 0 58 10 20 1 1 77 # ℹ 170 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Repeated Measures Example `ez::ezANOVA(data, dv, wid, within = NULL, between = NULL, type = 2)` ::: subpoint ○ `dv` = the outcome variable ::: ::: subpoint ○ `wid` = name of the column with subject identifier. Typically contains an `id` for each person (here, each chick!) ::: ::: subpoint ○ `within` = column(s) with within-subject factors ::: ::: subpoint ○ `between` = column(s) with between-subject factors ::: ::: subpoint ○ `type` = the sums of squares method used ::: `= NULL` means the default is set to `NULL`, and you do not necessarily need to input a value for that argument for the function to work. (May need to specify it for the function to work the way you *want*, though! Depends on your ANOVA goal.) ## Balanced or Unbalanced :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned |> count(week) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 week n 1 0 45 2 1 45 3 2 45 4 3 45 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} What type of Sums of Squares should we use? [Doesn't matter!]{.fragment} ::: :::: ## Repeated Measures Example `ez::ezANOVA(data, dv, wid, within = NULL, between = NULL, type = 2)` ::: subpoint ○ `dv` = the outcome variable ::: ::: subpoint ○ `wid` = name of the column with subject identifier. Typically contains an `id` for each person (here, each chick!) ::: ::: subpoint ○ `within` = column(s) with within-subject factors ::: ::: subpoint ○ `between` = column(s) with between-subject factors ::: ::: subpoint ○ `type` = the sums of squares method used ::: `= NULL` means the default is set to `NULL`, and you do not necessarily need to input a value for that argument for the function to work. (May need to specify it for the function to work the way you *want*, though! Depends on your ANOVA goal.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model <- ez::ezANOVA( data = chick_cleaned, dv = weight, wid = chick, within = week ) chick_weight_model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $ANOVA Effect DFn DFd F p p<.05 ges 2 week 3 132 184.9641 4.388747e-47 * 0.5768658 $`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity` Effect W p p<.05 2 week 0.006591028 2.933872e-44 * $`Sphericity Corrections` Effect GGe p[GG] p[GG]<.05 HFe p[HF] p[HF]<.05 2 week 0.375836 2.894679e-19 * 0.3789365 2.103585e-19 * ``` ::: ::: ## Assumptions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned |> pivot_wider(names_from = week, names_prefix = "week_", values_from = weight) |> select(starts_with("week")) |> cov() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` week_0 week_1 week_2 week_3 week_0 70.16364 215.8788 313.9909 318.0485 week_1 215.87879 1031.9495 1702.1818 1756.9066 week_2 313.99091 1702.1818 4357.6091 4694.9864 week_3 318.04848 1756.9066 4694.9864 5113.7192 ``` ::: ::: **Sphericity**: are the elements on the diagonal all equal in the population? **Compound Symmetry**: are the elements on the diagonal AND on the off-diagonals all equal in the population? ## Assumptions If assumption holds, `W` should be close to 1 and `p` will be large ($p > .05$). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model$`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity` ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Effect W p p<.05 2 week 0.006591028 2.933872e-44 * ``` ::: ::: ## Assumptions Corrections ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model$`Sphericity Corrections` ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Effect GGe p[GG] p[GG]<.05 HFe p[HF] p[HF]<.05 2 week 0.375836 2.894679e-19 * 0.3789365 2.103585e-19 * ``` ::: ::: ## Results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $ANOVA Effect DFn DFd F p p<.05 ges 2 week 3 132 184.9641 4.388747e-47 * 0.5768658 $`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity` Effect W p p<.05 2 week 0.006591028 2.933872e-44 * $`Sphericity Corrections` Effect GGe p[GG] p[GG]<.05 HFe p[HF] p[HF]<.05 2 week 0.375836 2.894679e-19 * 0.3789365 2.103585e-19 * ``` ::: ::: We observe a significant effect of week on chick weight. ## <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
